claims.text: As-received, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native oxide layer formed during storage or ambient exposure.
The native oxide layer on Q235 steel is transiently and partially protective in room-temperature and 700–900 °C salt environments.
The initial presence of the native oxide slows mass gain and corrosion-related degradation.
At high temperature, accelerated oxidation and thermal stresses can cause the native oxide to spall.
Spallation exposes fresh Q235 steel and causes corrosion to accelerate.
The native surface film may contain a mixture of iron oxides and oxyhydroxides.
At lower temperatures, the native oxide behaves as a self-healing, passivating barrier that retards further oxidation.
High temperature increases oxidation kinetics in Q235 steel.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide and Q235 substrate promotes oxide spallation.
Under room-temperature or mild conditions, oxide-intact samples should exhibit lower mass gain or slower degradation than oxide-removed samples.
During high-temperature salt exposure, the intact native oxide should initially delay corrosion.
Once the native oxide becomes unstable and spalls during high-temperature exposure, mass change and degradation should increase markedly.
Oxide-removed Q235 samples should exhibit a different high-temperature degradation profile from oxide-intact samples.
Engineered coatings such as atmospheric plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy coatings operate through mechanisms and thermal stabilities different from those of native Q235 oxide.
The proposed native-oxide mechanism may not apply to Q235 steel bearing engineered coatings or other robust surface treatments.
